First, we look at complexes created by dividing a finite graph into triangles by drawing an edge at random. Second, we consider complexes formed by dividing a finite planar map into triangles by drawing an edge at random. Both of these random complexes have some interesting properties. The first complex has a finite volume, is recurrent, and its boundary is a "critical percolating" set with a Hausdorff dimension of 4/3. Conversely, the planar map-based complex has a finite volume, is recurrent, and its boundary has a Hausdorff dimension of 5/2. Additionally, we prove that the boundary of the planar map-based complex has full measure. Another property examined is the nature of the "infinite cluster" in both types of random complexes. The first type has this cluster only at the infinite end point, whereas the planar map-based complex has this cluster on two ends. The boundary of the first type has a "Hitting time" of zero, whereas the boundary of the planar map-based complex has a "Hitting time" greater than zero. Lastly, we study the nature of the "resistance form" in these random complexes. The first type has this form discrete, multi-type, and monotone, whereas the boundary of the planal map-based complex has a "resistance form" continuous, multi-type, and monotone. Surprisingly, the two types of random complexes have a "resistance form" with the same total value.
